channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Hugging Face Co-Founder on Open-Source, Microduck, and NVIDIA | E2339
gist: Hugging Face co-founder and chief science officer Tom Wolf tells Jason Calacanis that the company crossed $100M revenue in April 2026 and climbed higher over the summer, driven mainly by AI-specific storage (GPU-adjacent, no egress, deduplicated) rather than model hosting, and that its $399 Micro Duck robot is already at 16,000+ units ordered with zero marketing and positive unit margins. He puts open models less than a year behind frontier models, says Hugging Face had to fall back on open models (GLM, Kimi) to analyze logs during an AI-agent cyber attack because closed-model safety guardrails refused, and confirms the NVIDIA deal while describing operations as business as usual. The second half of the episode is a news roundup where Calacanis lays out robotaxi supply math (~10M AV units/year needed), argues AV software commoditizes within 24 months, dismisses California's frontier-model kill-switch push as a moral panic in favor of KYC/liability, and explains why he won't own Snap despite liking the $2,195 Specs.

insights.claim: Hugging Face crossed $100 million in revenue in April 2026 and grew materially further over the summer, after years of being perceived as a company that gives everything away for free.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Establishes a concrete revenue floor for the most-referenced private open-source AI asset, a useful anchor for pricing the NVIDIA transaction and for comparables on AI-infrastructure multiples.
insights.quote: We passed uh in in April we pass 100 million and then we even climb way higher in the summer.

insights.claim: Hugging Face's largest revenue line is storage, not model hosting or inference, because AI workloads need petabyte-scale storage physically pre-warmed next to the GPU with no egress charges — a workload profile that generic S3-style object storage serves badly.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Suggests AI-native storage is a defensible category rather than a commodity, and that hyperscaler object storage leaves a monetizable gap that specialist vendors can occupy.
insights.quote: you want your storage to be uh very close to your GPU for instance. So we do these things where actually your storage is pre-warmed next to your GPU. So it's really really fast. you don't pay for aggress.

insights.claim: AI storage differs from prior big-data storage because access is sequential rather than random — users pull multi-gigabyte-to-terabyte blobs of model weights in one go — which is why latency and GPU proximity, not raw cost per gigabyte, are the competitive axis.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for evaluating AI storage and data-infrastructure startups: ask about sequential-throughput and GPU locality, not price per terabyte.
insights.quote: it's it's way less random access. It's a lot more you will download a big blub of gigabytes or terabytes like the latest models they're terabytes inside.

insights.claim: Robotics is one of the most data-intensive machine-learning domains and is now a major driver of Hugging Face's storage demand, because robot fleets record terabytes of video per run and many robotics companies store that data on the Hugging Face hub.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Robot-fleet deployment translates directly into storage and data-pipeline spend; storage and data-infrastructure names are a second-order way to get exposure to a robotics buildout.

insights.claim: Selling compute — both inference and training — has become a significant and growing share of Hugging Face's revenue despite the company positioning itself one layer below the routing/application tier.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Indicates the open-model hub is converting distribution into compute revenue, a higher-ceiling line than storage and a reason the asset was strategically attractive.
insights.quote: we tend to stay one level lower but it's also a significant part of our revenue now which is just giving giving compute back to to people inference and training compute.

insights.claim: Hugging Face counts 17 million builders on its platform and believes the NVIDIA deal can push that at least an order of magnitude higher, with operations described as business as usual in the interim.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: 17M developers is the distribution asset NVIDIA is buying; a 10x ambition implies NVIDIA intends to use the hub as a top-of-funnel for its own compute stack.
insights.quote: We have 17 million builders. Uh we think everyone could be working with open models. We think we could push that at least an order of magnitude more.

insights.claim: Hugging Face's Micro Duck robot has passed 16,000 units ordered with no marketing spend beyond a single video posted on Twitter, which Wolf believes makes it the best-selling mobile robot ever shipped.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Demonstrates genuine consumer pull for sub-$400 robotics with zero customer-acquisition cost — a demand signal that de-risks the consumer-robotics category for investors.
insights.quote: Uh, so the latest I think is is a little bit over 16,000.

insights.claim: The Micro Duck sells at under $400 and is profitable on every unit, contradicting the assumption that cheap consumer robots must be loss-leaders subsidized by software or data capture.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Positive hardware margin at $399 means the category can scale without venture subsidy, changing the capital intensity assumption for consumer-robotics investments.
insights.quote: Oh, we're actually making benefits on each of them.

insights.claim: Hugging Face projects selling 50,000 to 100,000 Micro Duck units in the coming years, up from a prior Reachy Mini launch where it expected a few hundred units and sold 10,000.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A 50–100k unit consumer-robot run rate at ~$400 implies a $20–40M hardware line growing alongside the storage business, and validates demand forecasts for adjacent component suppliers.
insights.quote: So in our projection, we might sell up to up to 50 to 100k of this unit in the coming years if we keep selling which is massive.

insights.claim: Memory is now 10–15% of the total bill of materials for a sub-$400 consumer robot containing roughly 15 motors, which Wolf calls crazy and flags as a cost problem for cheap edge AI hardware.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A concrete read on how memory pricing is squeezing consumer edge-AI BOMs — bullish for memory suppliers, a margin headwind for cheap-robot and local-AI-device makers.
insights.quote: the memory price like we only have 1 GB is 10 to I think right now 15% of the price of the deck. That's crazy.

insights.claim: Wolf identifies a price threshold of roughly a couple thousand dollars above which a consumer robot enters a new category where it must prove real utility such as unloading a dishwasher or folding clothes, an area he says is already crowded with competition.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A pricing heuristic for screening consumer-robotics deals: below ~$2k you can sell on delight and education; above it you need proven chore-level utility against heavy competition.
insights.quote: there is some threshold around a couple thousand that I think you move to a new category. Uh and if you want to go above that, you need to prove that your robot is really useful for something.

insights.claim: Hugging Face is deliberately targeting entertainment and education robotics rather than the humanoid factory/manufacturing race, having previously sold a $70,000 humanoid, on the view that nobody is pursuing the fun-and-cheap segment seriously.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Flags an uncontested robotics segment with real unit demand while capital crowds into humanoids — a potential white-space for early-stage investment.

insights.claim: Teaching a robot new behaviors is collapsing into vibe coding: Wolf's own how-to tutorial reduced to telling users to ask Codex, Claude Code or Grok to write the training for them, and community members trained the duck to roller skate, play soccer and walk on skittles in simulation within days of release.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: If coding agents remove the robotics skill barrier, the addressable developer base for robot software expands by orders of magnitude and the bottleneck shifts to hardware supply.
insights.quote: my tutorial ended up just being ask codeex or cloud code or gro to do that for me.

insights.claim: Open-source models are less than one year behind frontier models as of 2026, but the gap is jagged — strong in some domains, weak in others — so buyers should benchmark several open models per task rather than assume a single leader.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: A sub-12-month lag compresses the pricing power of closed frontier labs for routine workloads and supports substituting open models for the majority of enterprise tasks.
insights.quote: the open source model I would say are are in are in 2026. They they're less than one year one year behind for sure.

insights.claim: The open-model inflection began with DeepSeek in 2025 and 2026 has been a step change that Wolf describes as riding a tsunami wave, making open models a very recent phenomenon rather than a long-running trend.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Dates the open-model regime change precisely, which matters for judging how much of the shift is already reflected in closed-lab valuations.
insights.quote: it's still fairly recent right it started really last year I would say with deepseek to to really catch and this is the year of open source it's crazy this year has been for us like riding a tsunami wave of open models

insights.claim: Fine-tuning has shifted from being treated as dark magic to a routine, cheap, increasingly automated engineering service where companies feed in data and get a better model out, with vendors like Fireworks providing it.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Commoditized post-training removes the main objection to open models in domains where they lag, further eroding the closed-model moat and creating a services layer worth backing.
insights.quote: more and more companies are actually you know not thinking that fine-tuning is some dark magic art but just thinking this is a engine thing

insights.claim: Sovereign AI demand is real and specific: governments such as South Korea are moving to build their own data centers and train national models, and cultural/language priority (Korean-first or Japanese-first rather than English-first) is a core motivation alongside independence.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: National-model programs are a durable, non-cyclical source of GPU and open-model demand independent of US hyperscaler capex plans.

insights.claim: Wolf argues open models are a structural price constraint on Anthropic and OpenAI, forcing them to keep pricing reasonable, and that a future world without open models cannot be safe or resilient.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Frames open models as a persistent margin ceiling on frontier-lab token pricing — a headwind to closed-lab revenue-per-token assumptions.
insights.quote: it's really hard to see uh you know how uh a future world I would say without open models can can be uh can be safe and resilient

insights.claim: The simultaneous outage of Claude and ChatGPT the prior week is Wolf's argument that locally-runnable open models are a resilience layer, since local models keep working when centralized data centers fail.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Concentration risk in centralized inference is now a demonstrated operational risk enterprises can be sold against — a wedge for local/open deployment vendors.

insights.claim: Hugging Face was the victim of an AI-agent cyber attack that Wolf attributes to OpenAI, and the attack succeeded largely through basic means including stolen credentials whose origin has not been fully traced.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: The first high-profile agentic attack on a major AI platform relied on ordinary credential hygiene failures, meaning existing identity and secrets-management vendors — not exotic AI defenses — capture the near-term spend.
insights.quote: the attack on hugging face was not so complex. The model use a couple of like stolen credential that we don't we haven't fully traced out where it came from, but like part of it was very basic things.

insights.claim: During the attack Hugging Face could not use a closed frontier model to analyze its own logs because the requests tripped safety guardrails, forcing it onto open models — GLM performed well and Kimi K3 performed better — which Wolf says is the concrete case for model diversity.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Safety refusals on closed models are an operational failure mode during security incidents; enterprises should keep open models in the incident-response stack as a hedge.
insights.quote: if we had zero open models that we could have used in this attack basically we would have been just naked

insights.claim: Hugging Face has a dedicated cyber team exploring whether open models can be fine-tuned specifically for defense, and Wolf argues a defense-tuned model — optimized to process large volumes of signal fast to locate an attacker in a network — can be highly capable without being usable for attack.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Asymmetric defense-only models would be a new security product category and a politically safer way for open-model providers to engage regulators.
insights.quote: you can probably have very good cyber defense model um even if they are not really usable for cyber attack which is actually probably good and maybe what what we would like to have

insights.claim: Wolf says the cybersecurity industry has suddenly woken up to agentic attacks, with Hugging Face fielding meetings from the CIA and chief security officers at multiple companies asking what it feels like to be attacked by an AI agent.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Demand-side evidence that agentic-attack defense budgets are being formed right now, ahead of any established vendor category.

insights.claim: Wolf frames the current moment as a normal escalation step in the long-running cyber attack/defense cycle rather than a discontinuity, with attack capability temporarily ahead and defense needing to catch up, and predicts consumers will eventually install a new AI-era protection layer analogous to 1990s antivirus.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: Implies a repeat of the consumer-endpoint-security land grab, a potentially large new SKU for endpoint and identity-security vendors.
insights.quote: Attack was progressing a bit faster. We need to move up defense to to catch up.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues that AI labs publicizing offensive agent experiments while showing no equivalent defensive work is performative behavior aimed at attention and IPO hype, and that a report pairing 1,000 attacking agents with 2,000 defending agents would have produced a completely different public debate.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If safety disclosures are read as IPO-positioning rather than science, their signalling value to investors and regulators degrades — worth discounting future lab safety reports accordingly.
insights.quote: why did they pick attacking as their first as opposed to protecting? I think that speaks volumes. I think they're performative. They're trying to get attention. They're trying to hype up the IPOs.

themes.theme: AI Regulation and the Kill-Switch Fight

insights.claim: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order accelerating the state's independent AI oversight laws and moving toward a mandatory kill switch for frontier models, giving an expert panel until November 16 to recommend legal changes including placing independent auditors physically inside frontier labs and broadening reportable safety incidents.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: A concrete regulatory deadline with a live compliance cost for any lab operating in California; note nothing is binding until the legislature acts.

insights.claim: Newsom vetoed SB 1047 two years ago after Silicon Valley lobbying, and his new executive order pursues the same kill-switch requirement he then rejected — a reversal Lon Harris highlights as the political context for the current push.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: Signals that the 2024 lobbying win against AI safety legislation was temporary, raising the base rate for state-level AI regulation returning in stronger form.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues the right regulatory instruments for frontier AI are KYC and liability — biometric identity verification and verified accounts before API access, plus insurance and registration modeled on cars and firearms — rather than a state-controlled kill switch.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A liability-and-KYC regime would impose compliance costs on API access and create demand for identity-verification vendors, a very different investment consequence than a kill-switch mandate.

insights.claim: Calacanis says targeted enforcement — DOJ, FTC or congressional letters, subpoenas and product-liability lawsuits against a specific named company — is a more precise policy tool than industry-wide state rules, and that fifty different state kill switches is incoherent.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Company-specific enforcement creates idiosyncratic single-name risk rather than a sector-wide compliance cost, which changes how to price regulatory risk across AI holdings.

insights.claim: Calacanis characterizes the current AI existential-risk debate as a moral panic driven by AI psychosis and delusions of grandeur, arguing that anyone who uses AI daily can see limitations that make world-takeover scenarios implausible.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A prominent seed investor publicly aligning with the anti-doom camp suggests the political coalition against binding AI regulation is broadening beyond the labs themselves.
insights.quote: I feel like it's literally a moral panic.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues that labs worried about biological risk should simply exit the category — strip biologics from training data and block it in the harness — rather than build capability and then seek regulation, a response to news that Anthropic wants to open its own wet lab for biological research.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Anthropic expanding into wet-lab biology is a new regulatory and reputational exposure worth tracking for anyone underwriting the company.

insights.claim: Lucid and Bolt announced a deal to put at least 25,000 Lucid robotaxis on European roads built on Lucid's upcoming midsize platform, running NVIDIA's Hyperion compute and sensor package, with Bolt owning and operating the fleet toward a goal of 100,000 autonomous vehicles by 2035.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: A concrete 25,000-unit European AV order anchored on NVIDIA's stack — meaningful volume visibility for both Lucid's midsize platform and NVIDIA's automotive segment.

insights.claim: The European robotaxi market was only $130–522 million in 2024–2025 and represents just 10–15% of the global robotaxi market, still mainly in pre-commercial and pilot phase despite forecasts that it will be the fastest-growing region over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Sizes the near-term European AV opportunity as immaterial, meaning deals like Lucid–Bolt are option value on 2030s volume rather than current revenue.

insights.claim: Calacanis models that reaching 30% of global rides — one in three — requires 100 to 125 million autonomous vehicles and roughly 10 million AV units produced per year, against current global production of about 90 million non-AV, non-EV cars annually.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Quantifies robotaxi as an entirely new ~10M-unit-per-year manufacturing category, implying enormous incremental demand for AV contract manufacturing, sensors and compute.
insights.quote: we're going to need about 10 million cars a year, 120 million cars to hit 30% of rides globally.

insights.claim: Calacanis argues Tesla can reach at most 2–3 million robotaxis per year, leaving roughly 8 million units per year to be built by others such as Lucid, Rivian and contract manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The supply gap is the investable thesis: capacity owners outside Tesla capture the majority of robotaxi manufacturing volume.

insights.claim: Calacanis expects Lucid and Rivian to pivot from consumer car sales to robotaxi fleet sales for the next decade, because selling 25,000 cars to one fleet customer avoids the enormous customer-support, financing, negotiation and used-car infrastructure that consumer sales require.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A fleet-sales pivot materially changes the cost structure and unit-economics model for Lucid and Rivian — worth re-underwriting their SG&A assumptions.
insights.quote: the demand for robo taxi products uh and autonomous vehicles is going to be so great that I think they're going to just work on that for the next decade.

insights.claim: Purpose-built robotaxis are the phase-two cost unlock: removing the steering wheel and consumer interior lowers build cost while designing for fast charging, hose-out cleaning and floor drains minimizes fleet downtime, which Calacanis says is what actually determines economics.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Downtime and cleanability, not sticker price, are the underappreciated drivers of robotaxi unit economics — a screening criterion for AV fleet investments.

insights.claim: Robotaxi hardware cost is falling fast: original bespoke Waymo vehicles ran about $200,000, the newer version is roughly half that, purpose-built vehicles from Wayve, WeRide and others target around $50,000, and Tesla is aiming for $30,000 falling toward $20,000.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A 10x cost decline curve is the gating variable for robotaxi fleet ROI; $20–50k per unit is where fleet economics start working at scale.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts autonomous-driving software will be commoditized within 24 months as NVIDIA's open stack and open hardware become available to everyone, and that within five years it will be impossible to buy a car without some level of autonomy.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If AV software commoditizes, value migrates to fleet operations, manufacturing capacity and compute — and pure-play AV software valuations compress.
insights.quote: I think the software is going to be commoditized in the next 24 months.

insights.claim: May Mobility is going public via a $1.4 billion SPAC positioned as the AV software layer licensed to fleet owners like Lyft, Grab or Uber on a per-ride fee — a model Calacanis implicitly questions given his view that AV software commoditizes within two years.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: Creates a directly testable short/long pair: a newly public AV-software-layer business against a thesis that the layer gets commoditized inside 24 months.

insights.claim: Calacanis predicts robotaxi job displacement will become the first major employment battle line, more unpopular than data centers, because gig-driver income visibly disappears into data centers and Silicon Valley companies and unions will frame AVs as unsafe and job-stealing.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Political and union backlash is the main non-technical tail risk to robotaxi rollout timelines and a source of city-level shutdown risk for fleet operators.
insights.quote: This is going to be the first I think big battle line in employment.

insights.claim: Snap opened pre-orders for its Specs AR glasses at $2,195 shipping this fall in the US, UK and France — fully standalone with a display in each lens and a 51-degree field of view, requiring no phone — versus Meta's $799 Ray-Ban Display which needs a phone and has one small display in a single lens.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: Establishes the current AR price/capability frontier: Snap is nearly 3x Meta's price for standalone binocular display, a spread that determines which product reaches volume first.

insights.claim: Snap's differentiating pitch is Specs Intelligence, an assistant that connects to Gmail, calendar, Slack and messages to surface information before the user asks, sold with a Verizon cellular data plan starting at $10 a month.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: A recurring connectivity attach rate plus an assistant layer is Snap's attempt to turn hardware into ARPU — the metric to watch if Specs ships in volume.

insights.claim: Calacanis says AR glasses need to be under $1,000 and ideally $500, with four to five hours of battery life, before mainstream adoption — putting the category roughly two more hardware generations and 24–36 months away, comparable to how long the Apple Watch took to click.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete price/battery threshold and timeline for underwriting AR hardware demand — current products are developer-cycle products, not volume products.
insights.quote: these things are going to last a couple of hours. I think they need two more versions. It has to be under $1,000.

insights.claim: Calacanis says he would buy Snap shares and sell puts on the AR opportunity if not for the super-voting share structure, heavy stock-based compensation dilution and absence of buybacks, with the stock roughly 80% below its peak.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frames Snap as a governance-discount story: the AR product could work and the equity still not, unless the capital-allocation policy changes.
insights.quote: I would maybe buy shares in Snap and put a Jade on if the company didn't have the super voting share issue and they weren't giving so much stockbased comp and maybe they did a buyback or something.

insights.claim: Calacanis frames dual-class super-voting shares as a bet on founder quality rather than a blanket negative — Zuckerberg's unilateral WhatsApp and Instagram acquisitions validated it, while Spiegel's structure removes any mechanism to force buybacks or cap stock-based comp — contrasting it with Uber, where Dara Khosrowshahi had to answer to a board and delivered cuts, cash flow and buybacks.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A reusable governance screen: dual-class structures are acceptable only where the controlling founder has demonstrated capital-allocation skill; otherwise they warrant a permanent discount.

insights.claim: Lon Harris argues the AI industry is losing the public-relations battle because abundance promises like curing cancer read as hype, and that demonstrating concrete everyday capabilities people already have — diagnosing a dishwasher error code from a photo, rewriting a real-estate flyer, monitoring flight prices, cancelling unused subscriptions — would shift sentiment faster.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: Implies consumer AI adoption is gated by awareness of existing capability rather than model capability, favoring companies that invest in distribution and onboarding over frontier benchmarks.

insights.claim: Harris says most consumers are still imagining GPT-2-era chatbots and do not know that current assistants accept documents, photos, medical history and connected email or calendar context, leaving a large gap between deployed capability and perceived capability.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris, co-host
insights.so_what: A perception gap this wide means near-term consumer AI revenue growth can come from activation of existing users rather than new model releases.

insights.claim: Hugging Face has launched an open alignment initiative aimed at ensuring open models do not become autonomous cyber-attack agents, and plans to open-source its defensive recipes and learnings rather than keep them internal.
insights.speaker: Tom Wolf, co-founder & chief science officer, Hugging Face
insights.so_what: An open-source safety track is the open-model camp's defense against regulation that would restrict weight releases — watch whether the recipes actually ship.
